description: Somos Team Pedro Paulet, un equipo peruano apasionado por la ciencia, ingeniería, electrónica y exploración espacial. Tenemos conocimientos en programación, Python, ESP32, robótica, sensores, IoT y desarrollo de prototipos. Buscamos colaboradores con habilidades en inteligencia artificial, análisis de datos, diseño 3D, videojuegos, astronomía y desarrollo web. Valoramos la creatividad, el compromiso y el trabajo en equipo. ¡Construyamos juntos soluciones para el futuro!
summary:
KILLA NEVULA X is a pixel-art game, playable in the browser and on phones, where players design and fly a space mission from start to finish. The probe QUILLA went silent on the Moon: players build a rocket from compatible parts (engine, tank, frame, science bay, capsule), load fuel, oxygen, food and water within mass and budget limits, launch, repair a relay satellite on a spacewalk, land, find QUILLA and bring the crew home.

Every decision shows its cost before it is made and has consequences: run short on fuel and the capsule drifts. A single final evaluation scores science, fuel use, crew care, budget and time. The game offers three difficulty levels and local co-op for two players, and Pugberto, our mascot, shares NASA facts with their sources and stories of real scientists.

It matters because it turns the real trade-offs mission engineers face (mass, energy, risk and budget) into play, making mission design understandable and exciting for students.
details:
KILLA NEVULA X is an educational pixel-art game where players live every phase of a space mission, based on the NASA Mission Design Lab phases: briefing, design, build, launch, operations and debrief. The story is a rescue mission: the probe QUILLA lost contact on the Moon, and the crew must recover its data.

The lunar campaign has 10 levels:

  1. Mission Control: the player receives the mission goal.
  2. Hangar: build the rocket from compatible parts (engine, tank, frame, science bay, capsule and instruments) before time runs out. Every part has mass, cost and connector size.
  3. Supplies and launch: load fuel, oxygen, food and water without exceeding the engine’s capacity or the budget, then run the Go/No-Go poll and the ignition.
  4. The crossing: fix the communications link, share supplies with the crew and repair a relay satellite on a spacewalk by connecting cables, soldering and rebooting the transmitter.
  5. Landing: control the descent speed, sideways drift and tilt of the lander.
  6. Levels 6 to 9: on the lunar surface, triangulate QUILLA’s signal, set up a relay with line of sight to Earth, transmit the data and plan the trip home.
  7. Level 10: re-entry, parachutes and splashdown.

Every decision shows its cost before it is confirmed and has real consequences in the game. If fuel runs short, the capsule drifts; if the crew turns back early, the mission is marked as failed. At the end, a single evaluation (0 to 10) weighs science, fuel and energy, crew care, budget and time, with written feedback based on the player’s own decisions.

Benefits

  • Teaches the real trade-offs of mission design hands-on: mass vs. thrust, fuel vs. budget, risk vs. time.
  • Free to play in the browser, on computers and phones, with nothing to install.
  • Includes verified NASA facts, each with its source and link, presented by our mascot Pugberto, plus stories of real scientists and astronauts (Katherine Johnson, Margaret Hamilton, Franklin Chang-Díaz and more).
  • Clearly separates real data (“NASA Data”) from the game’s fiction.

Expected impact

We want high school and university students, and teachers in classrooms, to use the game to understand why a space mission needs planning, teamwork and evidence-based decisions. The two-player co-op mode encourages players to discuss and split roles, like a real mission team. Three difficulty levels make it useful from a first introduction to an advanced challenge. Because it runs on phones, it can also reach students without a computer.

Tools and technology

  • Engine: Unity 6 (6000.6.9f1), with the interface built in uGUI.
  • Language: C#.
  • Platform: WebGL build published on itch.io (https://alfredoms.itch.io/killa).
  • Mobile: touch controls with a virtual joystick and big buttons, in the style of games like Roblox.
  • Art: pixel art generated by code, with no third-party assets; the Pugberto character art was generated with Google Gemini.
  • Audio: music generated with the AI tool Suno; sound effects synthesized by code.
  • Data: public NASA data and pages, cited inside the game.
  • Development: the code was written with the help of an AI assistant (Claude by Anthropic); the design, decisions and testing were done by our team.
  • Quality: automated tests in Unity (Edit Mode) and an automated run through the whole game that renders screenshots.
  • Hardware: Windows laptops and PCs for development; tested in desktop browsers and on mobile phones.

Why is it creative?

  • Every technical phase of the mission becomes a different minigame: a race-against-the-clock hangar inspired by Overcooked, a landing bar inspired by fishing minigames and a first-person satellite repair.
  • Pugberto, an astronaut pug, guides the player, cheers them on, shares NASA facts and, depending on the difficulty, steals parts in the hangar, which adds humor and pressure.
  • Failure is not an abrupt ending: players see the consequences of their choices and a final evaluation that explains what went well and what did not.

Factors our team considered

  • Scientific accuracy: every NASA fact was checked against its source and is cited in the game.
  • Accessibility:
    • No warning relies on color alone: there is always an icon, text and a value.
    • Important instructions have high contrast.
    • Every action has a sound.
    • Long explanations are optional, behind “More info” buttons.
  • Inclusion: three difficulty levels. The easiest one adds hints, big buttons and automatically loaded supplies.
  • Teamwork: local co-op for two players on one keyboard, with different roles.
  • Access: runs on computers and phones, free and with no installation.
  • Responsible AI use: we disclose where AI was used (code, pixel art and texts with Claude, Pugberto’s art with Gemini, music with Suno), all images carry a visible “AI-assisted” watermark, and we do not use any NASA logos or branding.
  • Realistic scope: the Moon mission is complete from start to finish; Mars and Venus are planned as future expansions.
